mcqs.question: What allows an RNN to process sequences of any length with a fixed number of parameters?
options: It truncates every sequence to a fixed maximum length before training
It trains a separate set of weights for each possible sequence length
It uses the same weights at every time step, updating a hidden state passed forward
It only processes the first and last elements of the sequence
mcqs.explanation: Weight sharing across time steps is the key mechanism — the identical cell is applied at every step, with only the hidden state and current input changing, so parameter count never depends on sequence length. RNNs don't require truncation or per-length weight sets to achieve this.

mcqs.question: A vanilla RNN trained on 500-step sequences fails to learn a dependency between step 5 and step 490. What's the most likely root cause?
options: The hidden state is too large in dimension
RNNs cannot process sequences longer than 100 steps at all
The model was trained with too large a batch size
Gradients vanish (or explode) across the many repeated multiplications in backpropagation through time
mcqs.explanation: Backpropagation through time multiplies gradients repeatedly across every step going backward, and over hundreds of steps this reliably vanishes (or occasionally explodes) — the standard reason vanilla RNNs fail at long-range dependencies. Hidden state size and batch size aren't the core mechanism, and RNNs can technically process longer sequences, just poorly.

mcqs.question: You need strong long-range memory on a sequence task but have limited compute and training data. Which is generally the better starting point?
options: GRU, since it gives LSTM-comparable long-range memory with fewer parameters and gates
A vanilla RNN, since it has the fewest parameters
LSTM, since more gates always mean better performance regardless of data size
There is no meaningful difference between any of the three for this scenario
mcqs.explanation: GRU merges LSTM's three gates into two and its cell/hidden state into one, giving comparable long-range memory with less compute and fewer parameters to fit — a good match for a limited-data, limited-compute scenario. A vanilla RNN would fail at long-range memory, and LSTM's extra parameters aren't automatically better with scarce data.

mcqs.question: Why can't a bidirectional RNN be used for autoregressive text generation, even though it's standard for tasks like named entity recognition?
options: Bidirectional RNNs are simply too slow to ever be used at inference time
Generation produces tokens one at a time, so the 'future' context a bidirectional RNN's backward pass needs genuinely doesn't exist yet at the moment each token is generated
Bidirectional RNNs cannot be trained with backpropagation through time
Named entity recognition doesn't actually require any sequence context, so the comparison is meaningless
mcqs.explanation: The mismatch is structural: a bidirectional model's backward pass needs the full sequence already available, but during generation the tokens after the current position haven't been produced yet, so there's nothing for that backward pass to run over. It's not fundamentally a speed limitation, standard BPTT does train bidirectional RNNs fine, and NER very much relies on surrounding context, which is exactly why bidirectionality helps there.
